claim: Genome instability is a hallmark of aging and contributes to age-related disorders such as cancer and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Genome instability is a hallmark of aging and contributes to age-related disorders such as cancer and Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific consensus about aging and disease.

claim: The accumulation of DNA damage during aging has been linked to altered cell cycle dynamics and the failure of cell cycle checkpoints.
source: The accumulation of DNA damage during aging has been linked to altered cell cycle dynamics and the failure of cell cycle checkpoints.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge in the field about DNA damage and cell cycle regulation during aging.

claim: Age-associated genome missegregation events occur during aging in budding yeast.
source: Here, we use single cell imaging to study the consequences of increased genomic instability during aging in budding yeast and identify striking age-associated genome missegregation events.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1.

claim: The breakdown in mitotic fidelity results from the age-related activation of the DNA damage checkpoint.
source: This breakdown in mitotic fidelity results from the age-related activation of the DNA damage checkpoint and the resulting degradation of histone proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, particularly experiments with rad9∆ mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: The breakdown in mitotic fidelity results from the degradation of histone proteins.
source: This breakdown in mitotic fidelity results from the age-related activation of the DNA damage checkpoint and the resulting degradation of histone proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data with ies4∆ and tom1∆ mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Disrupting the ability of cells to degrade histones in response to DNA damage increases replicative lifespan.
source: Disrupting the ability of cells to degrade histones in response to DNA damage increases replicative lifespan and reduces genomic missegregations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Disrupting the ability of cells to degrade histones in response to DNA damage reduces genomic missegregations.
source: Disrupting the ability of cells to degrade histones in response to DNA damage increases replicative lifespan and reduces genomic missegregations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Histone degradation is beneficial to respond rapidly to damage but reduces lifespan and genomic stability in the long term.
source: We present several lines of evidence supporting a model of antagonistic pleiotropy in the DNA damage response where histone degradation, and limited histone transcription are beneficial to respond rapidly to damage but reduce lifespan and genomic stability in the long term.
evidence: This is a model supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence and inference from the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aneuploidy can be deleterious to fitness.
source: In particular, aneuploidy (the gain or loss of partial or whole chromosomes) can be deleterious to fitness (Beach et al., 2017; Sunshine et al., 2016) and has been implicated in many different types of cancers (Gordon et al., 2012) as well as developmental diseases such as Down Syndrome (Nagaoka et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aneuploidy has been implicated in many different types of cancers.
source: In particular, aneuploidy (the gain or loss of partial or whole chromosomes) can be deleterious to fitness (Beach et al., 2017; Sunshine et al., 2016) and has been implicated in many different types of cancers (Gordon et al., 2012) as well as developmental diseases such as Down Syndrome (Nagaoka et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2012.

claim: Aneuploidy has been implicated in Down Syndrome.
source: In particular, aneuploidy (the gain or loss of partial or whole chromosomes) can be deleterious to fitness (Beach et al., 2017; Sunshine et al., 2016) and has been implicated in many different types of cancers (Gordon et al., 2012) as well as developmental diseases such as Down Syndrome (Nagaoka et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Nagaoka et al., 2012.

claim: Formation of micronuclei can result in extensive damage and genomic rearrangements.
source: Recent work has also documented extensive damage and genomic rearrangements that can result following formation of micronuclei or from telomeric crisis (Maciejowski et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), and identified the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) sequences as particularly vulnerable to genomic damage (Flach et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Telomeric crisis can result in extensive damage and genomic rearrangements.
source: Recent work has also documented extensive damage and genomic rearrangements that can result following formation of micronuclei or from telomeric crisis (Maciejowski et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), and identified the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) sequences as particularly vulnerable to genomic damage (Flach et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ribosomal DNA (rDNA) sequences are particularly vulnerable to genomic damage.
source: Recent work has also documented extensive damage and genomic rearrangements that can result following formation of micronuclei or from telomeric crisis (Maciejowski et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), and identified the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) sequences as particularly vulnerable to genomic damage (Flach et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Flach et al., 2014 and Xu et al., 2017.

claim: Cells have robust surveillance mechanisms which arrest the cell cycle and promote repair in response to DNA damage.
source: To cope with DNA damage, cells have robust surveillance mechanisms which arrest the cell cycle and promote repair (Smith and Rothstein, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Smith and Rothstein, 2017.

claim: Double-stranded breaks are a particular challenge to cells and multiple breaks will quickly result in cell death if not corrected.
source: Double-stranded breaks are a particular challenge to cells and multiple breaks will quickly result in cell death if not corrected (Mehta and Haber, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mehta and Haber, 2014.

claim: The recognition of a double stranded break by the DNA damage checkpoint (DDC) is consistent across the cell cycle.
source: The recognition of a double stranded break by the DNA damage checkpoint (DDC) is consistent across the cell cycle, but there are subtle differences between repair mechanisms depending on the cell cycle stage (Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: There are subtle differences between repair mechanisms depending on the cell cycle stage.
source: The recognition of a double stranded break by the DNA damage checkpoint (DDC) is consistent across the cell cycle, but there are subtle differences between repair mechanisms depending on the cell cycle stage (Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of the DDC by a double stranded break causes increased chromatin mobility as a result of histone degradation.
source: Activation of the DDC by a double stranded break causes a host of changes to aid in DNA repair, including increased chromatin mobility as a result of histone degradation (Dion et al., 2012; Hauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2012 and Hauer et al., 2017.

claim: Extended activation of the DDC is detrimental to cells and has been linked to genomic instability and tetraploidization.
source: Extended activation of the DDC, however, is detrimental to cells and has been linked to genomic instability and tetraploidization (Davoli et al., 2010; Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davoli et al., 2010 and Davoli and de Lange, 2012.

claim: Genome instability is a hallmark of aging that occurs in many different species.
source: Genome instability is a hallmark of aging that occurs in many different species (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: The increase in genomic instability during aging is characterized by elevated rates of DNA mutations, loss of silencing, transposon activation, double-stranded DNA breaks, and changes to telomere maintenance.
source: This increase in instability is characterized by elevated rates of DNA mutations, loss of silencing, transposon activation, double-stranded DNA breaks, and changes to telomere maintenance (Sen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sen et al., 2016.

claim: Many progeric diseases which display apparent increases in the rate of aging are characterized by increased genomic damage and a reduced ability to repair DNA.
source: Furthermore, many progeric diseases which display apparent increases in the rate of aging are characterized by increased genomic damage and a reduced ability to repair DNA (Burtner and Kennedy, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Burtner and Kennedy, 2010.

claim: Chromosomal instability that results in aneuploidy is common during aging and could predispose cells to oncogenic transformation.
source: Chromosomal instability that results in aneuploidy is also common during aging and could predispose cells to oncogenic transformation (Naylor and van Deursen, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Naylor and van Deursen, 2016.

claim: Replicative lifespan is defined as the number of daughter cells produced by a mother cell prior to irreversible cell cycle arrest.
source: Replicative lifespan is defined as the number of daughter cells produced by a mother cell prior to irreversible cell cycle arrest (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Mortimer and Johnston, 1959.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells.
source: Several types of molecular damage have been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells, including mitochondrial dysfunction (Veatch et al., 2009), loss of vacuolar pH homeostasis (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), protein oxidation and misfolding (Hanzén et al., 2016), and instability at the rDNA (Ganley et al., 2009; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Veatch et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of vacuolar pH homeostasis has been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells.
source: Several types of molecular damage have been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells, including mitochondrial dysfunction (Veatch et al., 2009), loss of vacuolar pH homeostasis (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), protein oxidation and misfolding (Hanzén et al., 2016), and instability at the rDNA (Ganley et al., 2009; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hughes and Gottschling, 2012.

claim: Protein oxidation and misfolding have been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells.
source: Several types of molecular damage have been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells, including mitochondrial dysfunction (Veatch et al., 2009), loss of vacuolar pH homeostasis (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), protein oxidation and misfolding (Hanzén et al., 2016), and instability at the rDNA (Ganley et al., 2009; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hanzén et al., 2016.

claim: Instability at the rDNA has been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells.
source: Several types of molecular damage have been associated with replicative aging in yeast mother cells, including mitochondrial dysfunction (Veatch et al., 2009), loss of vacuolar pH homeostasis (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), protein oxidation and misfolding (Hanzén et al., 2016), and instability at the rDNA (Ganley et al., 2009; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ganley et al., 2009 and Sinclair and Guarente, 1997.

claim: The rDNA is a locus that experiences genome instability during replicative aging due to its makeup of 100–200 tandemly arrayed copies of an identical 9.1 kb repeat.
source: The rDNA, in particular, is a locus that experiences genome instability during replicative aging due to its makeup of 100–200 tandemly arrayed copies of an identical 9.1 kb repeat.
evidence: This statement combines established knowledge about rDNA structure with the observation of instability during aging.

claim: rDNA repeats are prone to recombination events that can lead to the formation of self-replicating, asymmetrically inherited extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs).
source: These repeats are prone to recombination events that can lead to the formation of self-replicating, asymmetrically inherited extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs), which accumulate in old mother cells (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sinclair and Guarente, 1997.

claim: ERCs accumulate in old mother cells.
source: These repeats are prone to recombination events that can lead to the formation of self-replicating, asymmetrically inherited extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs), which accumulate in old mother cells (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sinclair and Guarente, 1997.

claim: Recombination at the rDNA locus increases dramatically with age and has been strongly associated with loss of Sir2-dependent rDNA silencing and ERC accumulation.
source: Recombination at the rDNA locus increases dramatically with age and has been strongly associated with loss of Sir2-dependent rDNA silencing and ERC accumulation (Li et al., 2017; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2017 and Morlot et al., 2019.

claim: Deletion of the gene encoding the replication fork block protein Fob1 is sufficient to increase lifespan.
source: however, reducing the formation of ERCs and enhancing rDNA stability through deletion of the gene encoding the replication fork block protein Fob1 is sufficient to increase lifespan (Defossez et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Defossez et al., 1999.

claim: Overexpression of the sirtuin deacetylase Sir2 is sufficient to increase lifespan.
source: Overexpression of the sirtuin deacetylase Sir2, which also promotes rDNA stability and silences transcription within the rDNA (Saka et al., 2013), is similarly sufficient to increase lifespan (Kaeberlein et al., 1999), further supporting the model that rDNA instability contributes to replicative aging in yeast.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Saka et al., 2013 and Kaeberlein et al., 1999.

claim: Changes in silencing occur during yeast replicative aging.
source: Changes in silencing (Kaeberlein et al., 1999; McMurray and Gottschling, 2003) and alterations in nucleosome occupancy (Hendrickson et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2014) and chromatin remodelling (Dang et al., 2014) are thought to underlie some of the large-scale changes in gene expression during aging (Janssens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaeberlein et al., 1999 and McMurray and Gottschling, 2003.

claim: Alterations in nucleosome occupancy occur during yeast replicative aging.
source: Changes in silencing (Kaeberlein et al., 1999; McMurray and Gottschling, 2003) and alterations in nucleosome occupancy (Hendrickson et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2014) and chromatin remodelling (Dang et al., 2014) are thought to underlie some of the large-scale changes in gene expression during aging (Janssens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hendrickson et al., 2018 and Hu et al., 2014.

claim: Alterations in chromatin remodelling occur during yeast replicative aging.
source: Changes in silencing (Kaeberlein et al., 1999; McMurray and Gottschling, 2003) and alterations in nucleosome occupancy (Hendrickson et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2014) and chromatin remodelling (Dang et al., 2014) are thought to underlie some of the large-scale changes in gene expression during aging (Janssens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Dang et al., 2014.

claim: There is a reduction in the levels of key homologous recombination proteins during aging.
source: Among these changes in gene expression is a reduction in the levels of key homologous recombination proteins (Pal et al., 2018), however mutation accumulation does not appear to be a cause of replicative aging in yeast (Kaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Pal et al., 2018.

claim: Mutation accumulation does not appear to be a cause of replicative aging in yeast.
source: Among these changes in gene expression is a reduction in the levels of key homologous recombination proteins (Pal et al., 2018), however mutation accumulation does not appear to be a cause of replicative aging in yeast (Kaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kaya et al., 2015.

claim: During normal cell divisions in young cells, the amount of Htb2 in the mother cell nucleus increases during S-phase as histones are transcribed.
source: During each cell cycle, the amount of Htb2 in the mother cell nucleus increases during S-phase as histones are transcribed, and then drops as the cell enters mitosis and chromosomes are segregated to the newly formed daughter.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During normal cell divisions in young cells, Htb2 levels drop as the cell enters mitosis and chromosomes are segregated to the newly formed daughter.
source: During each cell cycle, the amount of Htb2 in the mother cell nucleus increases during S-phase as histones are transcribed, and then drops as the cell enters mitosis and chromosomes are segregated to the newly formed daughter.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vast majority of cell divisions in young cells follow the characteristic pattern of Htb2 increase during S-phase and decrease during mitosis.
source: The vast majority of cell divisions in young cells follow this characteristic pattern (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Abnormal segregation events become common as cells age.
source: As cells age, however, abnormal segregation events become common (Figure 1B, Videos 1–4, please ensure volume is on for all video playback to hear audio explanation).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1-4.

claim: GLM events result in cell cycle arrest that can range from a few minutes to many hours.
source: These genome-level missegregation (GLM) events result in cell cycle arrest that can range from a few minutes (Figure 1C-top) to many hours (Figure 1C-middle), before they are usually corrected by returning the aberrantly segregated genetic material to the mother cell.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GLM events are usually corrected by returning the aberrantly segregated genetic material to the mother cell.
source: These genome-level missegregation (GLM) events result in cell cycle arrest that can range from a few minutes (Figure 1C-top) to many hours (Figure 1C-middle), before they are usually corrected by returning the aberrantly segregated genetic material to the mother cell.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If GLM events are corrected, mother cells are able to proceed through subsequent divisions.
source: If corrected, mother cells are able to proceed through subsequent divisions, but if not, the mother cells will terminally exit the cell cycle and senesce (Figure 1C-bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: If GLM events are not corrected, the mother cells will terminally exit the cell cycle and senesce.
source: If corrected, mother cells are able to proceed through subsequent divisions, but if not, the mother cells will terminally exit the cell cycle and senesce (Figure 1C-bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mother cells retain an intact nuclear envelope during GLM events even when they appear to lose all of their chromatin.
source: The dynamics of the histone missegregation and recovery can be clearly seen in these time-lapse series, and strikingly the mother cells retain an intact nuclear envelope during these events – even when they appear to lose all of their chromatin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During GLM events, both spindle poles often fully enter the daughter rather than remain at the bud neck.
source: Interestingly, during these events, both spindle poles often fully enter the daughter rather than remain at the bud neck (Figure 1E), as can be seen by following the spindle component Spc72 (Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Video 2.

claim: In uncorrected, terminal GLMs, both spindle poles remained in the daughter cell during all observed events.
source: In uncorrected, terminal GLMs, both spindle poles remained in the daughter cell during all observed events (Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Video 2.

claim: Approximately three quarters of mother cells experience one or more GLMs during their replicative lifespan.
source: While most mother cells we observed experienced one or more GLMs, approximately 25% of wild type cells go their entire lives without a single event.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: When cells are young, they have a low probability of experiencing a GLM.
source: When cells are young, they have a low probability of experiencing a GLM; however, approximately three quarters of mother cells experience one or more GLMs during their replicative lifespan.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: As cells approach the end of life, the probability of a GLM increases dramatically.
source: Furthermore, as cells approach the end of life, the probability of a GLM increases dramatically (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Most GLM events are resolved within an hour.
source: The range of arrest durations is broad, with most events resolved within an hour, but some lasting many hours (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The duration of each GLM event is not affected by the age of the mother cell.
source: Interestingly, the duration of each event is not affected by the age of the mother cell (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: About 90% of GLMs are corrected successfully.
source: About 90% of GLMs are corrected successfully, allowing individual mother cells to live approximately 30% longer on average than if all GLMs were terminal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Individual mother cells live approximately 30% longer on average when GLMs are corrected compared to if all GLMs were terminal.
source: About 90% of GLMs are corrected successfully, allowing individual mother cells to live approximately 30% longer on average than if all GLMs were terminal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mother cells that undergo a GLM are more likely to die in the near future than cells of the same age that have not experienced such an event.
source: However, even when corrected, mother cells that undergo a GLM are more likely to die in the near future than cells of the same age that have not experienced such an event, and GLMs become increasingly predictive of impending mortality with increasing age (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: GLMs become increasingly predictive of impending mortality with increasing age.
source: However, even when corrected, mother cells that undergo a GLM are more likely to die in the near future than cells of the same age that have not experienced such an event, and GLMs become increasingly predictive of impending mortality with increasing age (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells that have undergone prior GLM events are more likely to undergo an additional event.
source: Similarly, cells that have undergone prior GLM events are more likely to undergo an additional event, indicating that there is a history dependence to GLM events and they do not occur in a completely stochastic manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: GLM events do not occur in a completely stochastic manner.
source: Similarly, cells that have undergone prior GLM events are more likely to undergo an additional event, indicating that there is a history dependence to GLM events and they do not occur in a completely stochastic manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing history dependence of GLM events.

claim: During GLMs where the majority of DNA enters the daughter cell, both Chr XII chromatids containing the rDNA repeats remain behind in the mother cell.
source: During GLMs where the majority of DNA enters the daughter cell, both Chr XII chromatids containing the rDNA repeats remain behind in the mother cell (Figure 2C,D, Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C, 2D and Video 6.

claim: During GLMs, Chr XII sister chromatids appear as a single point, only separating into two distinct foci following a GLM correction.
source: Furthermore, during these GLMs, Chr XII sister chromatids appear as a single point, only separating into two distinct foci following a GLM correction (Figure 2C, Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 6.

claim: Deletion of FOB1 reduces GLM rates compared with wild-type.
source: To explore whether the increase in GLM events during aging was primarily determined by rDNA instability during aging, we removed FOB1. These cells experienced a reduction in GLM rates compared with wild-type, but the age-related trend still held true even in fob1∆ cells (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: The age-related trend in GLM rates still holds true even in fob1∆ cells.
source: To explore whether the increase in GLM events during aging was primarily determined by rDNA instability during aging, we removed FOB1. These cells experienced a reduction in GLM rates compared with wild-type, but the age-related trend still held true even in fob1∆ cells (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: In fob1∆ cells, there was no reduction in the fraction of cells that died from a terminal missegregation despite increased replicative lifespan.
source: In spite of the increased replicative lifespan, there was no reduction in the fraction of cells that died from a terminal missegregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that rDNA instability is not the dominant cause of GLM events.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: rDNA instability is not the dominant cause of GLM events.
source: In spite of the increased replicative lifespan, there was no reduction in the fraction of cells that died from a terminal missegregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that rDNA instability is not the dominant cause of GLM events.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on fob1∆ cells.

claim: Deletion of MAD3 failed to alter the age-related increase in missegregation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we deleted the gene encoding the spindle assembly checkpoint component Mad3 (mammalian BubR1). This failed to alter the age-related increase in missegregation, and older mad3∆ cells had the same GLM rate as wild type cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Older mad3∆ cells had the same GLM rate as wild type cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we deleted the gene encoding the spindle assembly checkpoint component Mad3 (mammalian BubR1). This failed to alter the age-related increase in missegregation, and older mad3∆ cells had the same GLM rate as wild type cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Throughout the entire course of GLM arrest, spindles remained separated at a consistent 2–5 µm.
source: We quantified spindle pole separation during GLM events and throughout the entire course of the arrest, spindles remained separated at a consistent 2–5 µm (Figure 3A), similar to the mid-anaphase arrest identified by the Bloom lab (Yang et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The spindle separation during GLM arrest is similar to the mid-anaphase arrest identified by the Bloom lab.
source: We quantified spindle pole separation during GLM events and throughout the entire course of the arrest, spindles remained separated at a consistent 2–5 µm (Figure 3A), similar to the mid-anaphase arrest identified by the Bloom lab (Yang et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research supported by citations to Yang et al., 1997 and Yeh et al., 1995.

claim: Cdc14 is localized to the nucleolus for the majority of the cell cycle but exits the nucleolus to initiate anaphase.
source: To further determine whether cells had entered anaphase we monitored localization of Cdc14 (Figure 3C), which is localized to the nucleolus for the majority of the cell cycle but exits the nucleolus to initiate anaphase as part of the Cdc-Fourteen Early Anaphase Release (FEAR) and the Mitotic Exit Network (MEN) (Rock and Amon, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Rock and Amon, 2009.

claim: Cdc14 is specifically required for condensation and segregation of repetitive DNA sequences including the rDNA and telomeres.
source: Cdc14 is specifically required for condensation and segregation of repetitive DNA sequences including the rDNA and telomeres (D'Amours et al., 2004; Sullivan et al., 2004), and we hypothesized that this role could explain the Chr XII dynamics during GLMs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to D'Amours et al., 2004 and Sullivan et al., 2004.

claim: In 'normal' cell cycles Cdc14 begins to exit the nucleolus prior to division of genomic material between mother and daughter cells.
source: In 'normal' cell cycles Cdc14 begins to exit the nucleolus prior to division of genomic material between mother and daughter cells (Figure 3D, Video 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Video 7.

claim: In divisions where a cell undergoes a GLM, Cdc14 remains localized to the nucleolus during the GLM but is released immediately preceding correction.
source: In divisions where a cell undergoes a GLM, however, Cdc14 remains localized to the nucleolus during the GLM but is released immediately preceding correction (Figure 3D, Video 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Video 7.

claim: The continued localization of Cdc14 to the nucleolus during a GLM event indicates that the FEAR network has yet to initiate anaphase.
source: The continued localization of Cdc14 to the nucleolus during a GLM event indicates that the FEAR network has yet to initiate anaphase, and Cdc14 activation by FEAR precedes the return of genomic material to the mother.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations of Cdc14 localization.

claim: Cdc14 activation by FEAR precedes the return of genomic material to the mother.
source: The continued localization of Cdc14 to the nucleolus during a GLM event indicates that the FEAR network has yet to initiate anaphase, and Cdc14 activation by FEAR precedes the return of genomic material to the mother.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Checkpoint compromised rad9∆ cells experience essentially a complete abolition of terminal GLM events.
source: Checkpoint compromised rad9∆ cells experience essentially a complete abolition of terminal GLM events (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Following administration of zeocin, young cells experienced a dramatic increase in GLMs compared with control cells that are not exposed to zeocin.
source: Following administration of zeocin, young cells experienced a dramatic increase in GLMs compared with control cells that are not exposed to zeocin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GLM events are caused by activation of the DNA damage checkpoint.
source: This demonstrates that GLM events are caused by activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, and that the age-related increase in events is likely due to increases in genomic instability causing increased activation of the DNA damage checkpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zeocin experiment and rad9∆ data.

claim: The age-related increase in GLM events is likely due to increases in genomic instability causing increased activation of the DNA damage checkpoint.
source: This demonstrates that GLM events are caused by activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, and that the age-related increase in events is likely due to increases in genomic instability causing increased activation of the DNA damage checkpoint.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on rad9∆ and zeocin treatment.

claim: In rad52∆ cells, there is no age-related increase in GLM events, but instead a constant high-probability.
source: To do this we deleted RAD52 which performs functions analogous to mammalian BRCA2 in homologous recombination. In these rad52∆ cells, there is no age-related increase in GLM events, but instead a constant high-probability (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rad52∆ cells are more likely to suffer a terminal GLM than wildtype cells.
source: Although rad52∆ cells are more likely to suffer a terminal GLM than wildtype cells, this is not due to an increased rate of correction failure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increased likelihood of terminal GLM in rad52∆ cells is not due to an increased rate of correction failure.
source: Although rad52∆ cells are more likely to suffer a terminal GLM than wildtype cells, this is not due to an increased rate of correction failure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The GLM duration in rad52∆ cells is significantly longer than in wildtype.
source: Also intriguing is that the GLM duration in rad52∆ cells is significantly longer than in wildtype (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Homologous recombination is necessary to reduce both the frequency and duration of GLMs.
source: Thus, homologous recombination is necessary to reduce both the frequency and duration of GLMs, but Rad52-dependent homologous recombination does not affect the proportion of GLMs that can be repaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rad52∆ experimental data.

claim: Rad52-dependent homologous recombination does not affect the proportion of GLMs that can be repaired.
source: Thus, homologous recombination is necessary to reduce both the frequency and duration of GLMs, but Rad52-dependent homologous recombination does not affect the proportion of GLMs that can be repaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rad52∆ experimental data.

claim: Histone levels have been shown to influence replicative lifespan in yeast.
source: Histone levels have been shown to influence replicative lifespan in yeast (Feser et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2019), and recently activation of the DDC was found to cause a dramatic reduction in global histone levels (Hauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Feser et al., 2010 and Yu et al., 2019.

claim: Activation of the DDC was found to cause a dramatic reduction in global histone levels.
source: Histone levels have been shown to influence replicative lifespan in yeast (Feser et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2019), and recently activation of the DDC was found to cause a dramatic reduction in global histone levels (Hauer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hauer et al., 2017.

claim: In cells lacking TOM1, there is a significant reduction in GLM rates at the population level during aging.
source: In cells lacking either of these genes, there is a significant reduction in GLM rates at the population level during aging (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In cells lacking IES4, there is a significant reduction in GLM rates at the population level during aging.
source: In cells lacking either of these genes, there is a significant reduction in GLM rates at the population level during aging (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletions of TOM1 result in fewer cells dying from terminal missegregations.
source: Not only do these mutations result in reduced GLM rates, but fewer cells die from terminal missegregations (Figure 5B), and this is not a result of an increased fraction of GLM events that are corrected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletions of IES4 result in fewer cells dying from terminal missegregations.
source: Not only do these mutations result in reduced GLM rates, but fewer cells die from terminal missegregations (Figure 5B), and this is not a result of an increased fraction of GLM events that are corrected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletions of TOM1 do not come at a cost to replicative lifespan, but actually result in an increased lifespan.
source: Unlike mutations that compromise the DDC, however, deletions of TOM1 or IES4 do not come at a cost to replicative lifespan, but actually result in an increased lifespan (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Deletions of IES4 do not come at a cost to replicative lifespan, but actually result in an increased lifespan.
source: Unlike mutations that compromise the DDC, however, deletions of TOM1 or IES4 do not come at a cost to replicative lifespan, but actually result in an increased lifespan (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Histone transcription is tightly regulated and confined to S-phase.
source: Histone transcription is tightly regulated and confined to S-phase (Kurat et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kurat et al., 2014b.

claim: Deletion of HPC2 increases replicative lifespan.
source: Although deletion of HPC2 increases replicative lifespan and alters the dynamics of histone transcription, hpc2Δ cells do not have higher levels of histone proteins (Feser et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Feser et al., 2010.

claim: hpc2Δ cells do not have higher levels of histone proteins.
source: Although deletion of HPC2 increases replicative lifespan and alters the dynamics of histone transcription, hpc2Δ cells do not have higher levels of histone proteins (Feser et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Feser et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of HPC2 results in a significant reduction in terminal missegregation events.
source: Deletion of HPC2 results in a significant reduction in terminal missegregation events (Figure 6A), and also a reduced frequency of GLMs in aging cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of HPC2 results in a reduced frequency of GLMs in aging cells.
source: Deletion of HPC2 results in a significant reduction in terminal missegregation events (Figure 6A), and also a reduced frequency of GLMs in aging cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletion of SPT21 has been previously shown to reduce histone transcription and increase rDNA instability.
source: Deletion of SPT21 has been previously shown to reduce histone transcription and increase rDNA instability (Eriksson et al., 2012; Kobayashi and Sasaki, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Eriksson et al., 2012 and Kobayashi and Sasaki, 2017.

claim: Deletion of SPT21 caused an increase in terminal GLMs.
source: In contrast to deletion of HPC2, TOM1, and IES4, deletion of SPT21 caused an increase in terminal GLMs (Figure 6A) and an increased frequency of GLMs in mother cells (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of SPT21 caused an increased frequency of GLMs in mother cells.
source: In contrast to deletion of HPC2, TOM1, and IES4, deletion of SPT21 caused an increase in terminal GLMs (Figure 6A) and an increased frequency of GLMs in mother cells (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: Altering the temporal dynamics of histone transcription in aging cells is sufficient to modulate the frequency of GLM events both upward and downward.
source: These observations demonstrate that altering the temporal dynamics of histone transcription in aging cells is sufficient to modulate the frequency of GLM events both upward and downward.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on hpc2∆ and spt21∆ mutants.

claim: Deletion of BFA1 did not impact the frequency of GLM events during aging.
source: While deletion of BFA1 did not impact the frequency of GLM events during aging (Figure 7A), it significantly increased the fraction of GLMs that were not corrected and resulted in terminal missegregation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Deletion of BFA1 significantly increased the fraction of GLMs that were not corrected and resulted in terminal missegregation.
source: While deletion of BFA1 did not impact the frequency of GLM events during aging (Figure 7A), it significantly increased the fraction of GLMs that were not corrected and resulted in terminal missegregation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Neither activation of the spindle assembly nor the spindle positioning checkpoints result in GLMs.
source: Thus, neither activation of the spindle assembly nor the spindle positioning checkpoints result in GLMs, but the spindle positioning checkpoint is critical for healthy resolution of GLMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on mad3∆ and bfa1∆ mutants.

claim: The spindle positioning checkpoint is critical for healthy resolution of GLMs.
source: Thus, neither activation of the spindle assembly nor the spindle positioning checkpoints result in GLMs, but the spindle positioning checkpoint is critical for healthy resolution of GLMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on bfa1∆ mutants.

claim: Enhancing rDNA stability through deletion of FOB1 only delays, but does not substantially alter, the prevalence of GLMs or the capacity for cells to appropriately resolve GLMs.
source: However, our data indicate that enhancing rDNA stability through deletion of FOB1 only delays, but does not substantially alter, the prevalence of GLMs or the capacity for cells to appropriately resolve GLMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fob1∆ mutants.

claim: Loss of vacuolar pH has been identified as an early in life change that can result in a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Loss of vacuolar pH has been identified as an early in life change that can result in a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), which in turn has been linked to increased genomic instability during aging, likely through altered iron-sulfur cluster production and the resulting DNA replication stress (Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hughes and Gottschling, 2012.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential has been linked to increased genomic instability during aging, likely through altered iron-sulfur cluster production and the resulting DNA replication stress.
source: Loss of vacuolar pH has been identified as an early in life change that can result in a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012), which in turn has been linked to increased genomic instability during aging, likely through altered iron-sulfur cluster production and the resulting DNA replication stress (Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Veatch et al., 2009.

claim: The previously observed decline in histone abundance during aging likely results from DDC activation in aged mother cells.
source: Our data also illustrate how the previously observed decline in histone abundance during aging (Feser et al., 2010) likely results from DDC activation in aged mother cells, and that this protective response, which is beneficial in young cells upon exposure to DNA damaging agents (Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2012), leads to elevated rates of genome missegregation in old cells which eventually causes terminal senescence and death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and integration with prior research.

claim: DDC-mediated histone degradation is beneficial in young cells upon exposure to DNA damaging agents.
source: Our data also illustrate how the previously observed decline in histone abundance during aging (Feser et al., 2010) likely results from DDC activation in aged mother cells, and that this protective response, which is beneficial in young cells upon exposure to DNA damaging agents (Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2012), leads to elevated rates of genome missegregation in old cells which eventually causes terminal senescence and death.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; and Liang et al., 2012.

claim: DDC-mediated histone degradation leads to elevated rates of genome missegregation in old cells which eventually causes terminal senescence and death.
source: Our data also illustrate how the previously observed decline in histone abundance during aging (Feser et al., 2010) likely results from DDC activation in aged mother cells, and that this protective response, which is beneficial in young cells upon exposure to DNA damaging agents (Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2012), leads to elevated rates of genome missegregation in old cells which eventually causes terminal senescence and death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aging has been associated with an increased cell cycle time, and in particular an increased G1 duration.
source: Aging has been associated with an increased cell cycle time, and in particular an increased G1 duration.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In stem cells, elongated G1 is linked to increased DNA replication stress.
source: In stem cells, elongated G1 is linked to increased DNA replication stress (Flach et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Flach et al., 2014.

claim: In yeast, elongated G1 is thought to result from high levels of ERCs resulting in increased levels of the Rb analog Whi5.
source: In yeast it is thought to result from high levels of ERCs resulting in increased levels of the Rb analog Whi5 (Neurohr et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Neurohr et al., 2018.

claim: Reducing the G1 duration in yeast by overexpressing Cln2 fails to increase replicative lifespan.
source: Intriguingly, reducing the G1 duration in yeast by overexpressing Cln2 fails to increase replicative lifespan (Neurohr et al., 2018), but results in an improvement in single-strand annealing rates (Young et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Neurohr et al., 2018.

claim: Overexpressing Cln2 results in an improvement in single-strand annealing rates.
source: Intriguingly, reducing the G1 duration in yeast by overexpressing Cln2 fails to increase replicative lifespan (Neurohr et al., 2018), but results in an improvement in single-strand annealing rates (Young et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Young et al., 2019.

claim: At the single cell level, no connection was found between G1 duration and the occurrence of GLMs.
source: Surprisingly, however, at the single cell level we failed to find a connection between G1 duration and the occurrence of GLMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: A short G1 phase imposes constitutive replication stress in cycling stem cells.
source: For example, a short G1 phase imposes constitutive replication stress in cycling stem cells (Ahuja et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ahuja et al., 2016.

claim: The metaphase DNA damage checkpoint has been previously implicated in highly dynamic movements of the spindle poles prior to anaphase initiation.
source: The metaphase DNA damage checkpoint has been previously implicated in highly dynamic movements of the spindle poles prior to anaphase initiation (Palmer et al., 1989; Yang et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 2000; Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 1989; Yang et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 2000; and Yeh et al., 1995.

claim: In cells that experience a DNA double strand break, oscillations of the spindle poles and entry into the daughter have been previously reported, but only in the context of mutants with compromised DNA damage checkpoints such as chk1∆ or rad53∆.
source: In cells that experience a DNA double strand break, oscillations of the spindle poles and entry into the daughter have been previously reported, but only in the context of mutants with compromised DNA damage checkpoints such as chk1∆ or rad53∆ (Dotiwala et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Dotiwala et al., 2007.

claim: A recent report described segregation of the nucleus and spindle poles into the daughter cell in five aging yeast cells, which is likely to be the same phenotype detailed here.
source: Interestingly, a recent report described segregation of the nucleus and spindle poles into the daughter cell in five aging yeast cells, which is likely to be the same phenotype detailed here (Neurohr et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Neurohr et al., 2018.

claim: Responses to DNA damage have evolved under constraints of antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: Our findings suggest that responses to DNA damage have evolved under constraints of antagonistic pleiotropy, which refers to genes that have a beneficial effect during youth but whose activity results in detrimental effects later in life (Williams, 1957).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and supported by citation to Williams, 1957.

claim: Young (log phase) cells that are unable to degrade histones following DDC activation display an impaired ability to rapidly repair DNA damage and resume cell division following response to exogenous DNA damage.
source: Young (log phase) cells that are unable to degrade histones following DDC activation display an impaired ability to rapidly repair DNA damage and resume cell division following response to exogenous DNA damage (Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Hauer et al., 2017; and Liang et al., 2012.

claim: DDC-mediated histone degradation is likely to provide a selective benefit in young cells which may experience DNA damage due to environmental exposures.
source: Thus, DDC-mediated histone degradation is likely to provide a selective benefit in young cells which may experience DNA damage due to environmental exposures, for example.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior research.

claim: Activation of the DDC response due to age-associated genomic instability becomes detrimental.
source: However, activation of this response due to age-associated genomic instability becomes detrimental, and preventing histone degradation in response to DDC activation in aged cells both reduces GLMs and increases lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ies4∆ and tom1∆ mutants.

claim: Preventing histone degradation in response to DDC activation in aged cells both reduces GLMs and increases lifespan.
source: However, activation of this response due to age-associated genomic instability becomes detrimental, and preventing histone degradation in response to DDC activation in aged cells both reduces GLMs and increases lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on ies4∆ and tom1∆ mutants.

claim: Reducing the ability of cells to sense DNA damage (rad9∆) reduces the frequency of GLMs, but the cells are unable to respond to the damage and thus die younger.
source: Reducing the ability of cells to sense DNA damage (rad9∆) reduces the frequency of GLMs, but the cells are unable to respond to the damage and thus die younger.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on rad9∆ mutants.

claim: Reducing GLMs by increasing the levels of histone transcription (hpc2∆) increases the lifespan of cells as it reduces a negative consequence of DDC activation.
source: Reducing GLMs by increasing the levels of histone transcription (hpc2∆) or reducing the ability of cells to degrade histones (tom1∆, ies4∆), however, increases the lifespan of cells as it reduces a negative consequence of DDC activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on hpc2∆ mutants.

claim: Reducing GLMs by reducing the ability of cells to degrade histones (tom1∆, ies4∆) increases the lifespan of cells as it reduces a negative consequence of DDC activation.
source: Reducing GLMs by increasing the levels of histone transcription (hpc2∆) or reducing the ability of cells to degrade histones (tom1∆, ies4∆), however, increases the lifespan of cells as it reduces a negative consequence of DDC activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on tom1∆ and ies4∆ mutants.

claim: A decline in proteostasis, or the ability to ensure proper levels and folding of proteins, is one of the hallmarks of aging.
source: A decline in proteostasis, or the ability to ensure proper levels and folding of proteins, is one of the hallmarks of aging.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In yeast, activation of the proteasome through increased expression of Rpn4 is sufficient to increase lifespan and enhance proteostasis.
source: In yeast, activation of the proteasome through increased expression of Rpn4 is sufficient to increase lifespan and enhance proteostasis (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kruegel et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of Tom1 is sufficient to increase lifespan.
source: It is interesting, therefore, that deletion of Tom1, which is involved in proteostatic networks including histone maintenance (Singh et al., 2009) and ribosome quality control (Sung et al., 2016), is also sufficient to increase lifespan (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kruegel et al., 2011.

claim: Tom1 is involved in proteostatic networks including histone maintenance.
source: It is interesting, therefore, that deletion of Tom1, which is involved in proteostatic networks including histone maintenance (Singh et al., 2009) and ribosome quality control (Sung et al., 2016), is also sufficient to increase lifespan (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2009.

claim: Tom1 is involved in ribosome quality control.
source: It is interesting, therefore, that deletion of Tom1, which is involved in proteostatic networks including histone maintenance (Singh et al., 2009) and ribosome quality control (Sung et al., 2016), is also sufficient to increase lifespan (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sung et al., 2016.

claim: Approximately 25% of wild type cells go their entire lives without a single GLM event.
source: While most mother cells we observed experienced one or more GLMs, approximately 25% of wild type cells go their entire lives without a single event.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: The heterogeneity in GLM occurrence is under genetic control.
source: This heterogeneity is under genetic control, as demonstrated by mutations that both increase and decrease GLM frequency and penetrance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on various mutants.

claim: The likelihood that a GLM will be properly resolved in a given mother cell once it occurs appears to be variable and under genetic control.
source: Similarly, the likelihood that a GLM will be properly resolved in a given mother cell once it occurs also appears to be variable and under genetic control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on various mutants, particularly bfa1∆.

claim: Recent studies have indicated that aging yeast cells can experience different trajectories or 'modes' of aging.
source: Other recent studies have indicated that aging yeast cells can experience different trajectories or 'modes' of aging, as indicated by expression of reporter genes that differ within sub-populations of cells (Crane and Kaeberlein, 2018; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Crane and Kaeberlein, 2018; Jin et al., 2019; and Li et al., 2019.

claim: Genome instability is one of the nine 'Hallmarks of Aging' which are broadly evolutionarily conserved.
source: Although it remains unclear whether the specific mechanisms described here are shared during aging in multicellular eukaryotes, genome instability is one of the nine 'Hallmarks of Aging' which are broadly evolutionarily conserved (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: The DNA damage repair pathways and checkpoints are generally broadly conserved in evolution.
source: Likewise, the DNA damage repair pathways and checkpoints are generally also broadly conserved in evolution, and defects in these processes are associated with a variety of progeroid syndromes (Burtner and Kennedy, 2010; Lombard et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Burtner and Kennedy, 2010 and Lombard et al., 2005.

claim: Defects in DNA damage repair pathways and checkpoints are associated with a variety of progeroid syndromes.
source: Likewise, the DNA damage repair pathways and checkpoints are generally also broadly conserved in evolution, and defects in these processes are associated with a variety of progeroid syndromes (Burtner and Kennedy, 2010; Lombard et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Burtner and Kennedy, 2010 and Lombard et al., 2005.

claim: Aneuploidy and other major chromosomal rearrangements are ubiquitous in age-related human cancers.
source: Aneuploidy and other major chromosomal rearrangements are ubiquitous in age-related human cancers (Sansregret and Swanton, 2017), and there is accumulating evidence that rDNA is a key source of replication stress during aging across species (Flach et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sansregret and Swanton, 2017.

claim: There is accumulating evidence that rDNA is a key source of replication stress during aging across species.
source: Aneuploidy and other major chromosomal rearrangements are ubiquitous in age-related human cancers (Sansregret and Swanton, 2017), and there is accumulating evidence that rDNA is a key source of replication stress during aging across species (Flach et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Flach et al., 2014 and Pal et al., 2018.

claim: The INO80 subfamily is highly conserved from yeast to humans at both the protein and network topology levels.
source: The INO80 subfamily is highly conserved from yeast to humans at both the protein and network topology levels (Sardiu et al., 2015), so our findings are likely to have broad relevance to aging.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sardiu et al., 2015.

claim: The antagonistic pleiotropy between rapid and efficient response to DNA damage during youth coming at the expense of age-related declines in function and disease has been proposed in mammalian aging.
source: More generally, the antagonistic pleiotropy between rapid and efficient response to DNA damage during youth coming at the expense of age-related declines in function and disease has been proposed in mammalian aging (Rodier et al., 2007; Rufini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rodier et al., 2007 and Rufini et al., 2013.
